newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish security forces flex muscles in Islam row.
newsitem.headline: Turkish security forces flex muscles in Islam row.

text.p: Turkish police have raided outlawed religious education centres despite Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's bid to head off an anti-Islamist crackdown that has pushed his coalition to the brink of collapse.
Security officials said on Monday that police had swooped down on seven buildings in the western province of Bursa on Sunday where Islamists were teaching Koranic lessons without licences.
"The courses were closed," a spokesman for Bursa governor's officer told Reuters. "They were found to be operating outside the writ of the religious affairs directorate," he said.
The raids were the first confirmed report of concrete action since the secularist army demanded a crackdown against a religious revival two months ago.
A senior military officer voiced the generals' growing frustration at Erbakan's failure to heed their orders.

"The prime minister accepts everything in the National Security Council and says he agrees but then (Erbakan's Welfare Party) RP spokesmen outside say the complete opposite," the officer was quoted as saying in the Milliyet daily.

Two ministers from the conservative wing of the coalition resigned at the weekend, citing fears that Islamist Erbakan was steering NATO member Turkey away from its Western vocation and trying to enforce Islam in public life.

But their party leader, Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, on Monday reiterated her commitment to the government. "We will continue to work with stability," she told reporters after talks with Erbakan.
Ciller, a U.S.-educated secularist who was Turkey's first woman prime minister, says she is better placed to persuade the prime minister to toe the army's line from within the coalition.
Erbakan signed a communique issued by the military-dominated National Security Council on Saturday agreeing to go ahead with curbs on the role of Islam in public life.
However, senior Welfare MPs have vowed to block any bid by parliament to restrict religious education, a key army demand.
The military officer accused Erbakan -- secularist Turkey's first Islamist leader -- of "takkiye", a practice under which Moslems may hide their true feelings for the good of the faith.
"Erbakan is practising takkiye. He is trying to form a trap, play for time," he said.
Shares in Istanbul dropped 1.36 percent on Monday morning on concerns over the future of Erbakan's 10-month-old administration, brokers said. They recovered slightly in later trade.

The market, highly sensitive to Turkey's almost endemic political instability, lost 4.9 percent in one day last week after a press report that Ciller would pull her rightist True Path Party out of the coalition.
The military believe religious high schools, which would be marginalised under proposed education reforms, are producing a new breed of Islamists ready to infiltrate the secularist establishment.
The generals also say illegal Koranic courses, mostly prevalent in poor neighborhoods, openly encourage children to fight secularism.
Turkish televison showed pictures of policemen burning a wax seal over the door of one of the course buildings in Bursa. Bearded teachers in flowing Islamic robes looked on.
